conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/name: The Spanish and Portuguese conquest of the Americas
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/relig: The conquest was driven above all by the search for gold, silver, land and Indigenous labour, and by the ambitions of the Castilian and Portuguese crowns and of individual conquistadors. Yet religion was far more than decoration: the papal bulls of 1493 granted the new lands on condition that their peoples be evangelised, the Requerimiento made refusal of the faith a legal ground for war, and many conquistadors and friars sincerely believed they were extending Christendom and ending idolatry and human sacrifice. Bernal Díaz del Castillo summed up the mixture when he wrote that they came ‘to serve God and His Majesty, to give light to those in darkness, and also to get rich, as all men desire to do’. Historians such as J. H. Elliott and Matthew Restall stress this blend of motives; others, following Las Casas, emphasise how religious language legitimised plunder. The same Church also produced the conquest's sharpest critics.

conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/summa: Between 1492 and about 1600 Spain and Portugal conquered most of the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America, the Andes and coastal Brazil. Conquest was justified by papal grants and the duty to spread the gospel, and was accompanied by a ‘spiritual conquest’ of mass baptism and destruction of Indigenous religion. War, enslavement, forced labour and above all epidemic disease caused one of the greatest demographic collapses in human history — and provoked a fierce debate within the Church over whether such wars could be just.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/story:
In January 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella completed the conquest of Granada, the last Muslim state in Iberia, and in October of the same year Christopher Columbus, sailing for Castile, reached the Bahamas. Castile and Portugal brought to the Atlantic a crusading and Reconquista tradition in which conquest, settlement and conversion went together. In 1493 Pope Alexander VI's bull Inter caetera granted the Catholic Monarchs the newly found lands so that their inhabitants might be brought to the Christian faith, and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the non-Christian world between Castile and Portugal along a meridian in the Atlantic.

The first colony, on Hispaniola, became a laboratory of conquest. Taíno chiefdoms were defeated, tribute in gold was imposed, and Indigenous people were distributed to settlers under the encomienda, which made them labour for a Spaniard in return for supposed protection and instruction in the faith. Overwork, violence, hunger and disease shattered Taíno society within a generation. On the fourth Sunday of Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos preached in Santo Domingo that the settlers were in mortal sin for their cruelty. The crown responded with the Laws of Burgos (1512) and, in 1513, with the Requerimiento, a text drafted by the jurist Juan López de Palacios Rubios that conquistadors were to read before attacking, summoning the inhabitants to acknowledge the Church and the pope's grant to the Spanish monarchs on pain of war and enslavement. It was often read in Spanish, at a distance or to empty villages, and even contemporaries mocked it.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico with some 500 Spaniards. The decisive force in the fall of the Mexica empire was its Indigenous enemies, above all the Tlaxcalans, who supplied tens of thousands of warriors. At Cholula in October 1519 the Spaniards and their allies massacred thousands of unarmed people; in May 1520, during the festival of Toxcatl, Pedro de Alvarado's men slaughtered the Mexica nobility in the temple precinct of Tenochtitlan. The Spaniards were driven out on the Noche Triste (30 June 1520), but smallpox then swept through the city, and after a siege of some eighty days Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521, largely destroyed. Cortés smashed images in the temples, and Christian churches were built on the sites of pyramids.

In Peru Francisco Pizarro met the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532. The Dominican Vicente de Valverde presented him with a breviary and called on him to submit; when Atahualpa threw it to the ground, the Spaniards attacked and killed several thousand of his unarmed retinue. Atahualpa paid a vast ransom in gold and silver but was executed in July 1533, garrotted after accepting baptism. Manco Inca's great rising of 1536 besieged Cusco for months, and a neo-Inca state survived at Vilcabamba until 1572, when the viceroy Francisco de Toledo captured Túpac Amaru and had him beheaded in Cusco. Further conquests in Central America, Yucatán, New Granada and Chile continued for decades, and resistance never wholly ceased.

Military conquest was paired with a ‘spiritual conquest’. Twelve Franciscans arrived in Mexico in 1524, followed by Dominicans, Augustinians and later Jesuits; friars baptised Indigenous people in their hundreds of thousands, learned Nahuatl and other languages, and built a new Indigenous Christianity. They also destroyed temples, images and books: Bishop Juan de Zumárraga reported in 1531 the destruction of hundreds of temples and thousands of idols, and in 1562 the Franciscan Diego de Landa held an auto-da-fé at Maní in Yucatán in which Maya codices were burned and many Maya tortured on suspicion of idolatry. In Brazil, claimed for Portugal by Pedro Álvares Cabral in 1500, Jesuits led by Manuel da Nóbrega arrived in 1549; they gathered Indigenous people into mission villages, while governors such as Mem de Sá waged ‘just wars’ against the Tupinambá and settlers enslaved Indigenous captives for the sugar plantations.

The Church was also the main arena of protest. Bartolomé de las Casas, a former encomendero turned Dominican, spent half a century denouncing the conquest; Francisco de Vitoria at Salamanca argued that neither unbelief nor the pope's grant gave Spaniards a right to make war; Pope Paul III's bull Sublimis Deus (1537) declared that Indigenous peoples were true human beings who must not be enslaved. Charles V's New Laws of 1542 tried to phase out the encomienda, provoking a revolt of settlers in Peru, and in 1550–51 the crown suspended new conquests while a junta at Valladolid heard Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda debate whether war against the Indians was just. Philip II's ordinances of 1573 replaced the word ‘conquest’ with ‘pacification’, though practice changed more slowly.

By 1600 the Indigenous population of the Americas had fallen catastrophically, chiefly through smallpox, measles, typhus and other epidemics against which there was no immunity, but compounded by war, enslavement, forced labour, famine and social collapse. The labour shortage drove the transatlantic slave trade, which brought millions of enslaved Africans to the Caribbean and Brazil. Out of conquest came the Catholic Christianity of Latin America — the world's largest Catholic population today — shaped by Indigenous and African as well as Iberian traditions, and a lasting argument, begun by sixteenth-century friars, about the relation between the gospel and empire.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/nameO: Inter caetera (1493) granted the lands so that ‘barbarous nations be overthrown and brought to the faith’. The Requerimiento (1513) began with God's creation of the world and the pope's authority as Christ's vicar, and declared that the deaths and losses of those who refused would be their own fault. Conquistadors fought under banners of the cross and the Virgin and invoked St James (‘¡Santiago!’) as in the Reconquista; Cortés's banner reportedly bore the cross with the words ‘Friends, let us follow the cross, and with faith in this sign we shall conquer’. Victories were attributed to the Virgin and St James, mass baptisms followed conquest, and Sepúlveda argued that war was justified to end idolatry and human sacrifice and to open the way for preaching.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/relig: The papal bulls of 1493, especially Inter caetera, granted the Americas to Castile on condition of evangelising their peoples, giving conquest a religious legal title.
The Requerimiento of 1513 made refusal to accept the Church and the Spanish monarchs' authority a formal ground for ‘just war’ and enslavement.
A Reconquista mentality, completed in 1492 with the fall of Granada, linked the expansion of Christendom with conquest and settlement.

Many conquistadors and friars sincerely saw the destruction of ‘idolatry’ and human sacrifice as a Christian duty, and some friars hoped to build a purer, apostolic church among the Indigenous peoples.
Theologians such as Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda used Aristotle's theory of ‘natural slavery’ and the crimes of idolatry and sacrifice to argue that war against Indigenous peoples was just.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/other: The search for gold and silver — Hispaniola's placers, Aztec treasure, Atahualpa's ransom and, after 1545, the silver mountain of Potosí — was the dominant motive of most expeditions.
Conquistadors were private entrepreneurs seeking land, encomiendas, titles and social advancement, financing expeditions themselves in hope of reward.
Rivalry between Castile and Portugal, and later with France, England and the Netherlands, pushed both crowns to occupy and hold territory.
Indigenous political divisions — Tlaxcalan hostility to the Mexica, the Inca civil war between Atahualpa and Huáscar — supplied the conquerors with decisive allies.
The demand for labour on plantations and in mines drove slave-raiding and the encomienda, and later the importation of enslaved Africans.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/trigg: Columbus's landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492 and the establishment of a Castilian colony on Hispaniola in 1493.
Rumours of rich mainland empires, which drew Cortés from Cuba to Mexico in 1519 against the governor's orders.
Pizarro's contract (capitulación) with the crown in 1529 and the opportunity created by the Inca succession war.

Removed as governor in 1500 and sent home in chains; died in Valladolid still claiming his privileges.

Created Marquis of the Valley of Oaxaca but sidelined from government; died in Spain.

conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/casua: No credible figure exists for deaths caused directly by warfare. What scholars estimate is the overall collapse of the Indigenous population, most of it caused by epidemic disease (smallpox, measles, typhus and the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576) compounded by war, massacre, enslavement, forced labour and famine. Estimates of the pre-contact population of the Americas range from about 8–13 million (Ángel Rosenblat) to over 100 million (Henry Dobyns); a 2019 synthesis by Koch, Brierley, Maslin and Lewis suggested about 60 million, falling by roughly 90 per cent by 1600. For central Mexico, Cook and Borah's contested figures run from about 25 million in 1519 to about 1 million in 1605. The Taíno of the Greater Antilles had almost disappeared as distinct communities by the 1540s.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/effec: Spain and Portugal built vast American empires whose silver, sugar and other wealth transformed the world economy.
The Indigenous population collapsed by perhaps 90 per cent across the sixteenth century, largely through disease, with whole societies destroyed.
Labour shortages fuelled the transatlantic slave trade, which carried millions of enslaved Africans to the Americas.
New mestizo, Indigenous and African-Iberian societies emerged under a colonial caste hierarchy that shaped Latin America for centuries.
The debate over the conquest gave rise to the Salamanca school of natural law, the foundations of international law and early arguments for universal human rights.
The Catholic Church was established across the Americas under royal patronage (the Patronato Real and the Portuguese padroado), giving the crowns control of appointments and finance.

Mass baptism, the destruction of temples and codices and the extirpation of idolatry campaigns created a Christianity that often blended with Indigenous practice, notably around Our Lady of Guadalupe.
Friars produced grammars, catechisms and ethnographies in Indigenous languages, preserving much of the cultures they sought to replace.

The protest of Montesinos, Las Casas and Vitoria became a lasting Christian critique of conquest, later invoked by liberation theology and by modern papal apologies, such as John Paul II's in Santo Domingo in 1992 and Francis's in Bolivia in 2015.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/legac: The conquest of the Americas is the most consequential case of Christianity carried by conquest. It created the world's largest Catholic region and a rich Indigenous Christianity, but at the cost of devastation that the Church's own critics recognised at the time. Las Casas's writings fed both the Protestant ‘Black Legend’ against Spain and the development of natural rights, while modern churches in Latin America and Europe continue to wrestle with the ‘Doctrine of Discovery’, which the Vatican formally repudiated in 2023.
conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/disse: In his Advent sermon of 1511 in Santo Domingo he asked the settlers: ‘Are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Are you not obliged to love them as yourselves?’, and the Dominicans refused absolution to encomenderos who would not free their Indians.

Argued that the wars of conquest were unjust and the encomienda a mortal sin, that the gospel must be preached only by peaceful persuasion (De unico vocationis modo), and that the Spaniards owed restitution; his Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies (1552) catalogued the atrocities.

In his Salamanca lectures De Indis (1539) he denied that the pope had temporal dominion over the world or that refusal of the faith justified war, and held that the Indigenous peoples were true owners of their lands and polities.
His bull Sublimis Deus (1537) declared that the Indians were truly human, capable of the faith, and must not be deprived of liberty or property, even if they remained outside the faith.
Dominican bishop of Nicaragua who protested against the abuses of the governor's family and was murdered in León in 1550 for his defence of the Indigenous people.

conflicts/conquest-of-the-americas/campa: Christopher Columbus and the crews of the Santa María, Pinta and Niña

Columbus sailed from Palos in August 1492, refitted in the Canaries and reached the Bahamas on 12 October. After coasting Cuba he founded La Navidad on Hispaniola with the timbers of the wrecked Santa María; on his return in 1493 he found it destroyed and its garrison dead.
Hernán Cortés, about 500 Spaniards and thousands of Totonac and Tlaxcalan allies
Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz

Cortés scuttled his ships, won the Totonacs of Cempoala as allies, fought and then allied with Tlaxcala, massacred the people of Cholula and entered Tenochtitlan in November 1519. Driven out in June 1520, he regrouped in Tlaxcala, built brigantines for the lake and besieged the city until its fall in August 1521.
Pizarro's invasion of the Inca empire
Francisco Pizarro, his brothers and about 170 Spaniards

Landing at Tumbes, Pizarro founded San Miguel de Piura and climbed into the Andes to Cajamarca, where he seized Atahualpa in November 1532. After Atahualpa's execution the Spaniards marched south along the Inca road and occupied Cusco in November 1533.
